item.title: SemQBench: Benchmarking Decomposition-Aware Runtime Policies for Quantum-HPC Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.22886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors are increasingly used as accelerators inside high-performance computing (HPC) workflows. A workflow runtime decides which quantum circuits to run, how to group them into provider jobs, and what to repeat after a failed attempt. Many search problems split into independent parts, but the runtime can use that structure only when the workflow exposes the parts and a validity check for each one. SemQBench measures what a runtime gains from this visibility. It compares seven execution policies for the same search problem, including two controls without amplitude amplification. The policies change one runtime choice at a time: whether to amplify, whether partial results may be combined across runs, whether the parts share one circuit, and what a retry keeps. We run them on the 20-qubit IQM Garnet processor using 106 distinct circuits in three jobs, and report circuit executions, active device time, and provider jobs separately before combining them in a cost model. Amplifying the problem as one whole circuit shows no statistically clear gain over random sampling and uses 6.7-104$\times$ more active device time. Exposing the parts and collecting valid partial results across a fixed batch of runs cuts the executions needed for 95% completion confidence by 2.20-4.00$\times$, and this policy is never worse than the other amplified policies in executions, device time, or jobs; it is selected in 99 of 108 overhead settings. Fewer executions do not always mean less device time: on one workload, executions fall from thirteen to four while active device time rises from 7.44 to 9.81 $\mu$s. Exposing problem structure therefore gives the runtime a strong default policy and the measurements needed to decide when the simpler unamplified option is cheaper.
item.dc:creator: Chandrachud Pati, Yogesh Simmhan

item.title: An Embedded Industrial Irrigation System with Weather-Integrated Intelligent Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2610.23179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient irrigation management requires timely responses to soil moisture conditions and anticipated weather changes. This article presents an embedded, weather-based irrigation system that integrates soil moisture monitoring using multiple sensors, edge-based decision-making, automated pump control, and local data management. Four capacitive soil moisture sensors are connected to an STM32F103C8T6 microcontroller for data acquisition, while a BTT Pi V1.2 platform evaluates the sensor data, retrieves short-term weather forecasts, makes irrigation decisions, manages a graphical user interface, and stores operational data locally. Individual sensor readings serve as the basis for zone-level irrigation decisions, while the median of four time-averaged readings supports monitoring and analysis. Forecasted precipitation is taken into account as effective precipitation to reduce the calculated irrigation requirement before the pump is activated. The system was evaluated as part of a one-month cultivation trial with radishes, during which a total of 38,112 data points from measurement cycles were recorded. The median value of normalized soil moisture averaged 47.93\% and remained predominantly within the configured control range. Three irrigation events with a planned total irrigation volume of 26.68 L were recorded. Finally, we demonstrate the technical feasibility of integrating sensors, weather data, local data processing, automated control, and data collection into a scalable platform for precision irrigation.
item.dc:creator: Kiarash Zangooei, Arya Masoodpay, Hamid Reza Ghaeini

item.title: Surveying Experimentally-Validated Components for DNA-Based Molecular Communication
item.description: arXiv:2610.23361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular communication is a novel paradigm for the design of nanonetworks. It uses molecules as information carriers and enables communication between nanodevices. DNA-based molecular communication is a promising approach for medical applications, such as in-body networks for diagnostics and drug delivery. However, the transition from theoretical models to practical experiments is still in its early stages. This survey reviews experimentally validated DNA-tiles, nanocarriers, and biosensors relevant to implementing DNA-tile-based nanonetworks in vitro. We evaluate these components based on their stability, compatibility, cost-effectiveness, and overall suitability for wet-lab implementation. Based on this analysis, we identify promising component combinations and derive a blueprint for a minimal proof-of-concept experiment. The resulting framework provides researchers with both a structured overview of experimentally relevant design choices and a concrete starting point for implementing and validating DNA-based nanonetworks in the wet lab.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Waldner, Regine Wendt, Nils Stumpf, Sarah Scheer, Christian Hyttrek, Stefan Fischer, Florian-Lennert Lau

item.title: Agentic AI in Automated Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.22522v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). We study how heterogeneous agent behavior shapes stress, risk-adjusted performance, liquidity, and volatility in these types of markets. Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. Herd-followers produce the most frequent but shortest stress episodes, manipulators the fewest but most persistent, and rational agents the most stable rolling Sharpe ratios despite higher return volatility. SHAP attributions tie these patterns to drawdown and cross-asset signals, short-term volatility and position state, and momentum, respectively. The results motivate behavior-specific regulation rather than uniform limits on volatility or turnover.

item.title: Next Token or Vector? Learning How Far to Decode
item.description: arXiv:2610.22788v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, even when several upcoming tokens can be predicted together. We propose CADENCE (Context-Adaptive DEcoding), a generation method that learns both what to draft and how far to draft. Gaussian prediction heads represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, and a shared decoder converts the selected vector into token predictions in parallel. A learned router selects the prediction length from the model's own hidden states and predicted Gaussian parameters, adapting generation granularity to the current context with single-token generation as a fallback. The backbone verifies each proposed continuation and retains the prefix that matches its greedy predictions. Experiments with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval show that router-selected positions yield higher draft acceptance than applying the corresponding prediction length everywhere. CADENCE achieves up to 1.3x higher generation throughput than standard greedy decoding.
item.dc:creator: Sai Sreenivas Chintha, Chidera Biringa, Rishab Sharma, Anusha Agrawal, Prachi Badarayani, Gemma Zhang, Nigel Boachie Kumankumah, Marco Ayala, Sulaiman Vesal

item.title: Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.23466v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts, and tokens. We investigate whether network topology can identify transaction methods that describe DeFi operations. We extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.
item.dc:creator: C\'{e}lestin Coquid\'{e}, Alessio Brini, Natkamon Tovanich

item.title: HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advantage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for heterogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application-level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a calibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0--19.0$\times$ faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences' KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.
item.dc:creator: Jinheng Li, Guosheng Wang, Hongchao Du, Shangyu Wu, Qiao Li, Chun Jason Xue

item.title: Design-Space Exploration of Distributed Neural Networks in Low-Power Wearable Nodes
item.description: arXiv:2509.14540v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wearable devices increasingly support intelligent applications such as augmented reality, continuous health monitoring, and vision-based interaction. However, the neural networks (NNs) required by these applications often exceed the memory and energy budgets of wearable nodes. Cloud offloading reduces local computation but increases communication demand and can introduce latency and privacy concerns. TinyML reduces model complexity, potentially sacrificing accuracy without resolving the memory demands of vision workloads. This paper presents DistNN, a hardware-software framework for distributed NN inference that partitions execution between an ultra-low-power (ULP) wearable node and a nearby resource-rich hub, such as a smartphone. The node processes early NN layers and sends intermediate feature maps to the hub, which executes the remaining layers. To choose the split point, we propose a platform-independent figure of merit (FoM) based on data volume (DV) and cumulative computation cost (CC). The FoM captures the central trade-off: earlier splits reduce node computation but increase communication, whereas later splits reduce transmitted data but increase node computation. We also derive conditions for a net node-side energy benefit from distribution and demonstrate that the target autoencoder (AE) workloads cannot run monolithically on representative wearable microcontrollers. To enable ULP execution, we synthesize a custom node using low-precision fixed-point arithmetic. Post-synthesis estimates place DistNN below the 10 mW node-power target, with average node-compute power approximately 11x lower than that of the recent ML ASIC baselines evaluated. Across convolutional NNs and AEs, DistNN preserves task quality, achieving a structural similarity index (SSIM) of approximately 0.90 for image reconstruction with low-precision node features and a resource-rich hub decoder.
item.dc:creator: Meghna Roy Chowdhury, Ming-che Li, Archisman Ghosh, Md Faizul Bari, Shreyas Sen

item.title: Efficient LLM-Generated Shuttling Compilers for Complex Trapped-Ion Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2607.24714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers rely on shuttling compilers, which cast an input algorithm into a sequence of ion-qubit movements within a given architecture. We present the first study in which a single frontier large language model (LLM), Claude Opus 4.7, generates and iteratively refines the Python code of shuttling compilers from written specifications. Starting with a compiler for (i) a linear segmented trap, we extend it to (ii) a trap with junctions, and finally achieve efficient compilation for (iii) a broad class of connected trap graphs. The compilers for the more general cases are seeded with code from the previous ones. We benchmark the LLM-generated compilers against state-of-the-art hand-crafted ones using a common suite of quantum circuits. The number of shuttling timesteps is reduced by up to 72% for (i) and up to 43% for (ii). For the broad case (iii) of freely connected architectures, we find large variations in the required number of shuttling timesteps, depending on the connectivity. A densely connected, junction-rich architecture yields up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in shuttling timesteps compared to a corridor-like one. Repeating the complete generation and evaluation with a second frontier LLM, Claude Fable 5, reproduces these findings, with the Fable 5 compilers surpassing the hand-crafted ones more often on the largest circuits. Our results show that an unmodified frontier LLM can produce working, correct, and competitive shuttling compilers without additional manual algorithmic engineering. Generating compilers this way reduces the development time for new architectures from several months to a few days.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Kreppel, Reza Salkhordeh, Ferdinand Schmidt-Kaler, Andr\'e Brinkmann

item.title: Sufficient quantum provenance: retained fields and certified recording precision
item.description: arXiv:2610.09931v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum executions sharing a provenance record can produce different output distributions. We ask which execution details to retain, and at what precision, to guarantee agreement within a declared Hellinger tolerance. Under a specified channel model, we combine independent stochastic mechanisms and coherent rotation differences to certify recording precision without output simulation or explicit dependence on register dimension. For four-qubit quantum approximate optimization at depth one, a 13-bit comparison record suffices at tolerance 0.05 over a declared continuous noise range, uniformly in programmed angles for each fixed task. Pairwise separation constraints characterize sufficient field sets on finite context classes, exposing omissions that pass individually but fail jointly. Separately, six-qubit hardware measurements over six tested contexts certify minimum label counts of two for raw outputs and one after a fixed decoder, at tolerance 0.15 with 97\% simultaneous confidence under stationary independent shots. Execution records thereby carry checkable agreement guarantees.
item.dc:creator: George Kourousias, Sergio Carrato, Roberto Pugliese, Aljo\v{s}a Hafner, Francesco Guzzi, Matteo Bill\`e, Fulvio Bill\`e, Panagiotis Dimitrakis

item.title: Beyond Generation: Using Multimodal LLMs as Detectors of LLM-Generated Deepfake Facial Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.21760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As image generation models become increasingly capable of producing highly realistic content, traditional forensic techniques are struggling to keep up. This paper investigates whether MLLMs can instead be used as a form of forensic analysis by identifying synthetic media. Specifically, the study aims to determine whether these models detect fake images by recognising physical inconsistencies, or whether they rely on digital artefacts such as embedded watermarks. Six MLLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5, Gemini 3, and Seed 1.6) are benchmarked using a dataset of 400 images. Fifty images are authentic photographs, while the remaining 350 are generated using seven leading image models: Gemini 3, Gemini 2.5, Flux.2 Pro, GPT-Image-1, GPT-Image-1.5, Seedream 4.0, and Seedream 4.5. The evaluation is structured in three stages: single-image classification, pairwise comparison, and a focused "self-detection" experiment on Gemini. Several MLLMs achieved a high detection accuracy, with GPT-5.2 reaching a peak of 97.9% in the pairwise experiment, against specific generators and an overall mean pairwise accuracy of 82.5% by identifying structural or physical inconsistencies within images. However, results from the self-detection experiment indicate that the presence of invisible SynthID watermarks leads to a 10% reduction in Gemini's detection accuracy compared to the clean control group. One possible explanation is that SynthID embedding reduces some of the visible artefacts the models rely on for detection. These results imply that MLLMs can detect structural artefacts without relying on watermarks, but performance varies substantially across model generations. The findings also suggest that SynthID embedding may suppress some of the structural artefacts used during detection.
item.dc:creator: Olivia Salamon, Virginia N. L. Franqueira, Shujun Li
